paragraphs.heading: A planetary atom
paragraphs.text: The Bohr model, also called the Rutherford–Bohr model, is an outdated picture of the atom that brought in some early quantum ideas. It shows a small, dense nucleus with electrons orbiting around it. The layout resembles the Solar System, but electric attraction does the job that gravity does for planets. And the electrons may only have certain set energies, not any value at all: their energies are quantized.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: Niels Bohr developed the model between 1911 and 1918, building on Ernest Rutherford's discovery of the nucleus. It took over from Thomson's plum pudding model, and was itself replaced by the quantum atomic model in the 1920s. Compared with Rutherford's 1911 model, the main change was a new quantum interpretation taken from Haas and Nicholson. Bohr also gave up any attempt to explain radiation with classical physics.

paragraphs.heading: The problem to solve
paragraphs.text: In the late 1800s, some people imagined atoms as planetary systems with charged electrons in orbit. In 1897 Joseph Larmor showed, from classical electrodynamics, that an accelerating charge gives off power as radiation. An electron kept in orbit is always accelerating, so such an atom would be mechanically unstable. When Bohr started in 1912, Thomson's plum pudding model was the best available: rings of electrons inside a sphere of positive charge. But Thomson could not explain the many lines in atomic spectra.

paragraphs.heading: Rutherford's nucleus
paragraphs.text: In 1908 Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden showed that alpha particles sometimes scatter at large angles, which did not fit Thomson's model. In 1911 Rutherford explained this with a compact, highly charged mass at the atom's center. His scattering did not involve the electrons, so his picture of the atom was incomplete. Bohr opened his first paper by describing this atom: a small, dense, positive nucleus pulling on negative electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Explaining hydrogen's light
paragraphs.text: By the early 1900s, a good model of the atom was expected to account for its many spectral lines. Johann Balmer and Johannes Rydberg had summed these up in formulas drawn from measurements. The Bohr model's key success was explaining the Rydberg formula for the lines hydrogen gives off, which until then had no theory behind it. Another advance, the Rydberg–Ritz combination principle, tied line frequencies to differences between "terms", special frequencies typical of each element. Bohr read these terms as the atom's energy levels divided by the Planck constant. That led to the modern view that spectral lines come from differences in energy.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is still taught
paragraphs.text: Today the Bohr model counts as an obsolete theory. It can be obtained from quantum mechanics, which is broader and far more accurate, as a first-order approximation of the hydrogen atom. But it is simple and gives correct results for some systems. So it is still used to introduce students to quantum mechanics and to energy level diagrams.
